lesson.title: Forces and Motion: PhET Net Force Investigation
lesson.buzzAssessmentTitle: Unit 3 Lesson 1: Forces and Motion - PhET Net Force Investigation

gradingDesign.rule: Only lessons with a completed provided chart use 10 automatic points; variable student evidence is graded in the final two BusyBee responses.

questions.prompt: In the required Net Force setup, two 50 N blue pullers pull left. What is the total force pulling left? ________ N
In the same setup, one 150 N red puller pulls right. What is the total force pulling right? ________ N
What is the magnitude of the net force for 100 N left versus 150 N right? ________ N
Which direction does the net-force arrow point in the required setup?
After you press GO for the required setup, what happens to the cart?
What is the correct physics term for a change in velocity?
On the Motion screen, what happens while 100 N is continuously applied to the 200 kg refrigerator?
In the required Motion-screen trial, what happens after the applied force returns to 0 N?
Compare one balanced setup with the required unbalanced setup. State the forces, net force, and motion evidence you observed in each.
questions.rubricText:
@[Always] Grading feedback: Use evidence from two named PhET setups and distinguish force balance from motion.
a. Full credit: Correctly describes a balanced setup with zero net force and no acceleration, and compares it with 100 N left versus 150 N right, a 50 N rightward net force, and rightward acceleration.
  Partial credit: Gives the correct comparison but omits one force value or one motion observation.
  No credit: Does not compare balanced and unbalanced evidence or reverses the net-force direction.

questions.prompt: Explain how your evidence from both the Net Force and Motion screens supports Newton's First and Second Laws. Include the required 50 N net-force setup and the refrigerator trial.
questions.rubricText:
@[Always] Grading feedback: Connect both screens to the laws using specific force and motion evidence.
a. Full credit: Uses the 50 N rightward net force to explain acceleration, uses the 200 kg refrigerator trial to connect force, mass, and acceleration, and explains that zero net force produces no acceleration or approximately constant velocity.
  Partial credit: Correctly explains both laws but uses incomplete evidence from one screen.
  No credit: Gives definitions without lab evidence or makes an incorrect force-motion claim.
